title: Identify the physical constituent of astronomical dark matter

concept.text: Identify the physical entity or entities responsible for the matter inferred from astronomical gravitational effects, and establish how their measured properties account for that cosmic component. Gravitational observations reveal the influence of dark matter without uniquely determining what it consists of. The innovation would connect those observations to identifiable constituents whose relevant properties can be measured.

Scope synthesis: finding a new particle in a detector would be an important step, but identifying astronomical dark matter also requires a quantitative connection between that particle and the abundance and distribution inferred in the universe. The goal allows multiple constituents. Identifying a component that supplies only a small fraction would establish part of the answer while leaving the broader accounting unfinished. The supplied evidence concentrates on weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs; that experimental focus does not establish that WIMPs exhaust the possible constituents.

significance.text: Identifying the constituents and establishing their astronomical contribution would turn a gravitationally inferred component of the universe into a physical system with measurable properties. It would connect the matter shaping cosmic structure to microscopic physics. The possibility of discovering new fundamental physics has a concrete basis in WIMP searches: the reviewed LZ paper describes WIMPs as candidates motivated by theories beyond the Standard Model. New fundamental physics remains a possible consequence, rather than a necessary outcome of every conceivable identification.

Conditional impact synthesis: measured constituent properties could make explanations of cosmic structure more predictive by replacing some assumptions about dark matter with experimentally constrained inputs. Depending on the constituent, this could inform models of structure formation and the early universe. Identification alone would not explain every feature of galaxies, remove uncertainties in ordinary matter and its evolution, or guarantee a practical technology. Its immediate revolutionary value would be explanatory and experimental.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is obtaining evidence that both identifies a constituent and distinguishes it from competing physical explanations. Astronomical gravitational effects do not uniquely specify microscopic properties. Conversely, detector interpretations depend on models: the reviewed LZ search calculates recoil spectra using different microscopic interactions together with an assumed Standard Halo Model. A detector signal interpreted under such assumptions does not independently measure the full cosmic abundance and distribution.

A concrete experimental barrier is separating an extremely rare candidate interaction from rare backgrounds while maintaining a reliable statistical model. The reviewed LZ paper documents uncertainty in extrapolating an electron-capture background into the tail of its distribution, with that systematic uncertainty omitted from the statistical inference. This matters because an apparently unusual event can become less persuasive if a relevant background is incompletely modeled. Improving sensitivity must therefore be accompanied by background characterization and independent confirmation.

Scientific synthesis: the astronomical barrier is closing the inference from a measured interaction to the amount and behavior of the constituent in the universe. A convincing account would need to test whether inferred constituent properties remain compatible with independent astronomical observations, distinguish measured quantities from halo assumptions, and establish whether additional components are required. Agreement within one interaction model or one assumed halo would leave important alternatives unresolved.

current_state.text: The supplied evidence documents an unresolved identification problem and a specific experimental hint. The reviewed LZ webinar dated December 8, 2025 distinguishes dark matter's gravitational detection from its unknown particle properties and explains that direct detection could allow those properties to be studied. This establishes the motivation for the search; it does not report identification of a constituent.

On September 1, 2026, LZ reported one unusual event in its extended-energy nuclear-recoil search. The reviewed paper reports a maximum local significance of 3.4 sigma and a global significance of 2.6 sigma after accounting for look-elsewhere effects—the increased opportunity to obtain an apparently unusual result when searching across alternatives. The global result is well short of a discovery. Both the supplied saved LZ homepage and the dated Stanford report retain the 2.6-sigma result; the earlier assertion that the homepage had removed it is incorrect.

The September result is represented in the supplied evidence by an LZ preprint, a collaboration announcement and Stanford reporting. The reviewed paper describes the analysis as non-blind, and the supplied material does not establish subsequent peer-reviewed publication or independent replication. A statistical fluctuation or an unaccounted-for background remains possible. The significance is conditional on the tested statistical and background models, including the documented limitation in the electron-capture background treatment. Stanford's approximately 0.5% wording must not be read as the posterior probability that the event was caused by background, or as a probability that dark matter has been discovered.

Evidence boundary: these dated materials support the September report and its cautions, but the supplied review contains no bounded freshness-search entries establishing whether subsequent developments changed the assessment by November 1, 2026. The homepage snapshot was retrieved on November 11, 2026; that retrieval date does not establish comprehensive coverage of intervening research. The reviewed artifacts were reported as fully extracted without truncation or extraction problems, and the assessment did not depend on visual inspection of figures. These limits leave later developments unresolved rather than invalidating the dated result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: obtain reproducible astronomical or nongravitational evidence that identifies a constituent and constrains the properties needed to interpret its astronomical role. A laboratory route should establish a repeatable signal with independently tested background explanations and consistent physical interpretation across additional observations or experiments. An astronomical route should distinguish the proposed constituent from credible alternatives. These are proposed criteria for this record, not published consensus standards or an accomplished demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible evidence identifies a constituent and constrains relevant properties

completion_criteria.text: Proposed astronomical accounting: show quantitatively that the identified constituent's properties and inferred population explain the relevant dark-matter abundance and distribution in independent observations. Make assumptions about interaction models and halo structure explicit, and test how conclusions change when those assumptions vary. If evidence establishes a mixture, account for the components collectively; identifying only a subdominant constituent would constitute partial completion.
completion_criteria.label: Constituent properties and population explain dark-matter abundance and distribution

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope boundary: make the data, calibration, background treatment and inference sufficiently available for independent scrutiny, and seek confirmation with different systematic uncertainties where feasible. State which observations, environments and parameter ranges have been explained and which remain open. Finite tests can establish demonstrated breadth and consistency, but cannot prove that one constituent explains every dark-matter phenomenon everywhere. No universal numerical discovery or accounting threshold is established by the supplied review.
completion_criteria.label: Available data and methods enable scrutiny within stated explanatory limits

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis—AST-04, Establish the physical cause of cosmic acceleration: both concepts seek the physical explanation of a major cosmological inference. AST-03 concerns the constituent or constituents of gravitationally inferred matter; AST-04 concerns the cause of accelerated cosmic expansion. Identifying dark matter would not by itself establish the cause of acceleration.

Roster synthesis—AST-07, Discover a reproducible breakdown of general relativity near black holes: both involve interpreting gravitational observations and testing physical explanations. AST-03 seeks a constituent accounting for astronomical dark matter, while AST-07 requires reproducible evidence that general relativity fails in a particular regime. A result in either area could constrain the other's interpretation, but neither demonstration automatically completes the other.

Roster synthesis—AST-06, Map the cosmic dark ages and first luminous structures in three dimensions; AST-11, Identify the first generation of metal-free stars; and AST-13, Establish how the earliest massive black holes formed and grew: these remain separate observational and explanatory goals concerning early cosmic structure. Identified dark-matter properties could improve their physical modeling, while observations of early structure could constrain dark-matter models. None of those achievements alone identifies a dark-matter constituent.

Roster synthesis—AST-05, Detect and identify a primordial gravitational-wave background, and AST-12, Directly detect the cosmic neutrino background: these share the goal of connecting cosmological inference with identifiable physical signals. AST-05 targets a primordial gravitational-wave background; AST-12 targets relic neutrinos. Their detection could constrain cosmological models, but neither should be equated with identifying the constituents responsible for the astronomical dark-matter component.

Roster synthesis—AST-09, Make neutrino astronomy capable of routinely resolving hidden cosmic sources, and AST-10, Open the millihertz gravitational-wave sky as a working observatory: these concern sustained observational capabilities in different messengers. They overlap with AST-03 in rare-signal detection, background control and inference, while their completion depends on resolving sources or operating an observatory rather than identifying dark matter.

Roster synthesis—AST-01, Establish that an exoplanet hosts life; AST-02, Detect an independently verifiable extraterrestrial technology; AST-08, Produce resolved surface maps of rocky exoplanets; and AST-14, Establish the physical energy budget of coronal heating: these have more distant connections through astronomical measurement and interpretation. Each retains its own target—life, technology, planetary surfaces or coronal heating—and none is a prerequisite for identifying dark matter.

unresolved_issues: Whether later results changed the September 2026 assessment by November 1, 2026 is unestablished because no bounded freshness-search entries were supplied.
The supplied material does not establish subsequent peer-reviewed publication or independent replication of the September result.
The unusual LZ event remains compatible with a statistical fluctuation or an unaccounted-for background; its physical origin is unresolved.
The review documents a background-tail systematic uncertainty omitted from the statistical inference, but does not establish its quantitative effect on the reported significance.
The evidence concentrates on WIMP searches and does not provide a comprehensive assessment of other possible constituent classes.
The supplied record establishes neither a constituent's quantitative cosmic contribution nor whether dark matter comprises one component or a mixture.

brief.title: Knowing what dark matter is made of
possible: We could identify the matter whose gravity helps shape galaxies, then measure its properties. Dark matter would become something we can study physically, rather than something we know through its gravitational effects alone.
why: Scientists could connect the matter shaping cosmic structure to the physics of its constituents. Measured properties could replace some assumptions in explanations of how structure formed and how the early universe evolved.

sources.showed: LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) observed an unusual event consistent with a nuclear recoil, meaning a nucleus knocked by a particle, where expected background signals were low.
sources.quote: We observe one event with characteristics consistent with a nuclear recoil
sources.cited_for: LZ has reported a possible signal in its search for dark matter.
sources.not_established: The event does not identify dark matter or establish how much of it exists in the universe.

sources.showed: LZ reported a possible interaction involving a weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP: a hypothetical heavy particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.
sources.quote: A new LZ study found one particle interaction that is difficult to explain with known background processes and could potentially have been caused by a WIMP.
sources.cited_for: The unusual interaction remains a hint that further measurements could strengthen or weaken.
sources.not_established: The result falls short of a discovery and could still reflect chance or an unaccounted-for background.

shown: LZ has reported an unusual detector event in a preprint. It remains a hint, without established independent confirmation. Its interpretation depends on how well researchers account for background signals from ordinary matter.
missing: Reproducible evidence must identify a constituent and distinguish it from credible alternatives.
Measured properties and the inferred population must account for dark matter’s amount and distribution across independent observations.
Data, calibration and background models must support independent scrutiny and confirmation.

milestones.label: Repeatable evidence identifies a constituent and its properties
milestones.explanation: Repeatable evidence would have to identify a constituent, constrain its relevant properties and withstand alternative explanations. This would establish what contributes to astronomical dark matter.

milestones.label: The constituents explain dark matter’s amount and distribution
milestones.explanation: The constituents’ properties and inferred populations would have to explain dark matter’s amount and distribution across independent observations. This would connect their identity to their cosmic contribution.

milestones.label: Independent scrutiny establishes what the explanation covers
milestones.explanation: Accessible data and methods would have to support independent scrutiny, with confirmation under different sources of error where feasible. Clear limits would establish which observations the explanation covers.

uncertain: The LZ event’s physical cause remains unknown, and the effect of an omitted background uncertainty on its statistical strength is unresolved.
Dark matter may contain several constituents; identifying a minor component would leave the broader accounting unfinished.
No universal numerical threshold defines when identification and cosmic accounting are sufficient.

page.title: Identification of the constituents of astronomical dark matter
page.definition: The physical constituent or mixture responsible for dark matter—matter inferred from astronomical gravitational effects—is identified. Its measured properties and inferred population account quantitatively for the cosmological abundance and astronomical distribution attributed to dark matter.

goal.need: In the standard cosmological model, the cosmic microwave background implies about 5.4 times as much cold dark matter as ordinary matter. Gravity maps where that mass lies, yet different constituents can produce a similar shortage of small structures. Knowing the constituent and its properties would let astronomers test which physical process shaped the distribution of galaxies. Interpreting their inner structure would still require accounting for the effects of ordinary matter.

figures.caption: Planck’s inferred present-day matter densities
figures.note: Values assume Planck’s base ΛCDM model: a spatially flat cosmology with a cosmological constant and cold dark matter. Ω is density divided by critical density; h is the Hubble constant divided by 100 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹.

completion.title: Identified constituents account for dark matter’s cosmological abundance and astronomical distribution.
completion.criterion: Independent experiments or observations establish the constituent identities. Their measured properties and inferred populations jointly account for the cosmological dark-matter density and its distribution in independent astronomical observations, within the uncertainties of an explicitly specified joint model. Contributions from multiple constituents are accounted for collectively. Identification of a subdominant component constitutes partial completion. No universal numerical agreement tolerance is assigned.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of the identification, verification, abundance and structure-formation tasks stated in P5, APPEC and Snowmass reports.
completion.basis: Searched P5, APPEC, PDG and Snowmass documents and direct-search conventions for a universal identification criterion, required constituent fraction and numerical abundance or distribution tolerance; none was found. Snowmass distinguishes verification, measurement of constituent properties, determination of the fraction supplied and explanation of structure formation. This test combines those tasks without inventing a numerical threshold.

milestones.title: A direct particle search finds an excess with a global significance of at least 3σ.
milestones.criterion: The data reject the background-only hypothesis at a global significance of at least 3σ, equivalent to a one-sided p value of about 1.35 × 10⁻³ or less. When the search scans signal hypotheses, the global p value includes the chance of finding an excess at least as significant anywhere in that scan.
milestones.set_by: Direct-dark-matter-search community convention documented by Baxter et al., section 4.1; the recommendation was written for direct particle searches.
milestones.threshold_quote: Claims of evidence should require at least a \(3\sigma \) global discrepancy with the background-only hypothesis.

milestones.title: A search for a new particle finds a candidate signal with a significance of at least 5σ.
milestones.criterion: A search for a new particle finds an excess over its background-only prediction at a significance of at least 5σ, equivalent to a one-sided p value of about 2.87 × 10⁻⁷ or less. If the search scans signal hypotheses, distinguish the significance at the selected hypothesis from the significance over the scan. Connecting the particle to astronomical dark matter requires independent evidence.
milestones.set_by: Particle-physics discovery convention described by CERN in “12 steps – From idea to discovery”; its stated scope is new-particle searches.
milestones.threshold_quote: A “discovery” is claimed when the statistical significance of the excess (the “bump”) is at least 5 sigma.

milestones.title: Other experiments verify a candidate dark-matter signal.
milestones.criterion: An experiment independent of the original observation detects a signal consistent with the same candidate. For measurements of the same particle property, the inferred values must be statistically compatible. Snowmass specifies no numerical replication significance.
milestones.set_by: Snowmass 2013 dark-matter complementarity group, “Complementarity of Dark Matter Experiments”, section 27.6.

milestones.title: Complementary measurements determine a detected constituent’s share of astronomical dark matter.
milestones.criterion: Complementary measurements identify the detected constituent’s relevant properties and determine whether it supplies all dark matter or a measured portion. The result must distinguish an inferred constituent abundance from a dark-matter density assumed when interpreting a signal. Snowmass specifies this qualitative result without a required fractional precision. Establishing a portion leaves the remaining abundance and the collective explanation of astronomical structure for completion.
milestones.set_by: Snowmass 2013 dark-matter complementarity group, “Complementarity of Dark Matter Experiments”, conclusions; the published formulation concerns particle candidates.
milestones.threshold_quote: to determine whether the particle makes up all of dark matter or only a portion

milestones.title: A laboratory recoil search excludes combinations of particle mass and scattering cross section.
milestones.criterion: Use measured detector data to exclude a region of particle mass and scattering cross section, the quantity that sets the probability of scattering from the target. State the confidence level, the interaction tested and the assumed Galactic halo density and velocity distribution.
milestones.set_by: APPEC Dark Matter Direct Detection Committee, scientific objectives of direct detection. The exclusion of mass and interaction ranges is a qualitative objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: to experimentally exclude the broadest accessible ranges of both quantities

milestones.title: Stellar microlensing sets a 95% upper limit on the Galactic halo fraction in compact objects.
milestones.criterion: Use the rate and durations of stellar magnification events, corrected for detection efficiency, to bound the fraction of the Milky Way dark halo mass in compact lenses at 95% confidence as a function of lens mass. Specify the halo model, lens mass distribution and treatment of events attributable to ordinary stars.
milestones.set_by: Microlensing survey convention applied by OGLE and compared with EROS and MACHO limits in figure 10 of Mróz et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: 95% upper limits on the fraction of dark matter in the form of PBHs and other compact objects.

milestones.title: Measurements determine a detected particle’s mass and interaction cross section.
milestones.criterion: For a particle detected through scattering, infer its mass and scattering cross section from the signal and complementary measurements. Report the interaction model and the dependence of the inference on the local dark matter density.
milestones.set_by: APPEC Dark Matter Direct Detection Committee, scientific objectives of direct detection.
milestones.threshold_quote: to determine its mass and interaction cross section

milestones.title: Complementary measurements determine how much astronomical dark matter a detected particle supplies.
milestones.criterion: Infer the particle’s abundance and compare it with the independently inferred cosmological dark matter abundance, propagating uncertainties under the stated model. The comparison must distinguish a particle consistent with supplying all dark matter from one measured to supply only a portion. A halo density fixed as an input to a scattering analysis supplies no independent abundance measurement.
milestones.set_by: Snowmass 2013 dark-matter complementarity group, conclusions. The group specifies no fractional precision.
milestones.threshold_quote: to determine whether the particle makes up all of dark matter or only a portion

not_found: No universal completion criterion specifying a constituent fraction and numerical abundance or distribution tolerance was found.
No independent replication or subsequent peer-reviewed publication of LZ’s 1 September 2026 event report was located through 14 November 2026.
No P5, APPEC or Snowmass statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of constituent identification as a whole.

results.finding: OGLE microlensing of nearly 35 million Magellanic Cloud stars puts a 1% upper limit on the halo fraction in planetary-mass compact objects.
results.detail: The authors used a flat prior on the halo fraction and a zero-event Poisson likelihood for compact lenses. They rejected a short brightening as a likely stellar flare and omitted the SMC halo from the rate model.

case_label = "Candidate class". Reason: Particle scattering and gravitational lensing test distinct classes of proposed constituents.

goal.need = "In the standard cosmological model, the cosmic microwave background implies about 5.4 times as much cold dark matter as ordinary matter. Gravity maps where that mass lies, yet different constituents can produce a similar shortage of small structures. Knowing the constituent and its properties would let astronomers test which physical process shaped the distribution of galaxies. Interpreting their inner structure would still require accounting for the effects of ordinary matter.". Reason: The density ratio gives the scale of the problem, but the existing paragraph leaves unexplained why a better mass map alone cannot settle how dark matter shaped galaxies.

add statement by Astroparticle Physics European Consortium (APPEC), Dark Matter Direct Detection Committee, 2021: "DM particle interactions with a detector should be given top priority in astroparticle physics". Reason: Recommendation 1 identifies direct detection as the specific particle-search goal endorsed by APPEC.

add not found: "No P5, APPEC or Snowmass statement was found disputing the value or feasibility of constituent identification as a whole.". Reason: The roadmaps distinguish uncertainty about individual search methods from opposition to identifying dark matter.
add case "Particle candidates". Reason: Particle evidence can be assessed against the search conventions that apply to the measured interaction.
add case "Compact objects". Reason: Microlensing surveys test compact-object populations, including primordial black holes, through their gravitational effects on background starlight.

add milestone after None: "A laboratory recoil search excludes combinations of particle mass and scattering cross section.". Reason: A laboratory detector can exclude candidate masses and interaction strengths before any excess appears, as the early germanium experiment demonstrated.

edit m1: title = "A direct particle search finds an excess with a global significance of at least 3\u03c3."; criterion = "The data reject the background-only hypothesis at a global significance of at least 3\u03c3, equivalent to a one-sided p value of about 1.35 \u00d7 10\u207b\u00b3 or less. When the search scans signal hypotheses, the global p value includes the chance of finding an excess at least as significant anywhere in that scan."; threshold_quote = "Claims of evidence should require at least a \\(3\\sigma \\) global discrepancy with the background-only hypothesis."; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5]. Reason: The 3σ recommendation applies to direct searches, and an excess over background does not by itself establish the particle interaction asserted in the old title.

edit m2: title = "A search for a new particle finds a candidate signal with a significance of at least 5\u03c3."; criterion = "A search for a new particle finds an excess over its background-only prediction at a significance of at least 5\u03c3, equivalent to a one-sided p value of about 2.87 \u00d7 10\u207b\u2077 or less. If the search scans signal hypotheses, distinguish the significance at the selected hypothesis from the significance over the scan. Connecting the particle to astronomical dark matter requires independent evidence."; threshold_quote = "A \u201cdiscovery\u201d is claimed when the statistical significance of the excess (the \u201cbump\u201d) is at least 5 sigma."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 5, 4]. Reason: CERN describes a new-particle discovery convention, while the direct-search recommendations decline to set a discovery threshold and the DAMA example tests modulation.

edit m3: criterion = "An experiment independent of the original observation detects a signal consistent with the same candidate. For measurements of the same particle property, the inferred values must be statistically compatible. Snowmass specifies no numerical replication significance."; threshold_quote = "verification by other experiments."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 8]. Reason: The COSINE-100 and ANAIS-112 comparison is an experimental result and obscures the criterion for successful verification.

add milestone after m2: "Stellar microlensing sets a 95% upper limit on the Galactic halo fraction in compact objects.". Reason: The compact-object case lacks the mass-dependent halo-fraction test already used by independent microlensing surveys.

split m4 into "Measurements determine a detected particle’s mass and interaction cross section." | "Complementary measurements determine how much astronomical dark matter a detected particle supplies.". Reason: Measuring a particle’s properties and inferring its share of dark matter are separate results, since interpreting the first measurement can require assuming a halo density.

structure = parallel. Reason: A compact-object survey can constrain the halo fraction independently of any laboratory excess, and a new-particle search can reach discovery significance independently of a direct-search signal.
remove not found 1. Reason: The statement that the numerical milestones apply only to particle searches becomes inaccurate once the microlensing limit is included.
